newsitem.title: QATAR: Gulf Arabs to welcome Iraq's return to oil markets.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs to welcome Iraq's return to oil markets.

text.p: Gulf Arab leaders are expected to welcome Iraq's limited return to world oil markets but they appear relatively confident their earnings will not be drastically eroded, delegates said on Sunday.

Delegates attending the annual Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) summit in Qatar told Reuters the group would welcome Baghdad's resumption of limited oil exports to ease the suffering of fellow Arab Iraqis.

But they are not expected to collectively respond favourably to Iraqi overtures for reconciliation, delegates said. GCC states hold Iraq's Saddam Hussein responsible for the hardships his people are facing by failing to meet U.N. demands to earn at least the partial lifting of sanctions.
The GCC, which groups OPEC majors Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Qatar with small independent oil producers Oman and Bahrain, is due to issue a final statement on Monday.
Iraq has said it would be ready to export oil on Tuesday for the first time since the United Nations imposed crippling sanctions against Baghdad for invading Kuwait in 1990.

Various GCC ministers are holding side talks at the December 7-9 summit to discuss political, economic and military integration but the oil ministers are not present, a sign of little concern at Iraq's return causing a major drop in world prices.

When prices were falling in 1993 GCC oil ministers held emergency talks during the summit in Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter and producer, and offered to cut production if other world producers did the same.

But this year even GCC member Kuwait has welcomed the Iraqi deal with the United Nations to sell oil worth $2 billion over a renewable six month period to pay for food, medicines and some U.N. operations linked to the 1990-91 Gulf crisis.

GCC states have been suffering budget deficits in recent years mainly due to weak oil prices and the huge costs of the 1991 Gulf War aganist Iraq but current prices are about $8 a barrel higher than last year despite OPEC's overproduction.
January Brent futures contract closed on Friday at $24.54 a barrel while most GCC had calculated their revenues for 1996 at a conservative weighted average price for their crudes of $13-$15 a barrel.
According to a Reuters survey OPEC pumped 26.08 million barrels per day in November, about a million bpd above the quota which includes Iraq.
